segments.speaker: doctor
segments.text: Hi, Mr. Mitchell, I'm Dr. Raman. Good to see you again. Before we start, can you confirm your date of birth for me?

segments.speaker: patient
segments.text: July 19th, 1967.

segments.speaker: doctor
segments.text: Thank you. And we have your address as 1187 Birchwood Drive, Missisuga, L5G 2K9. Is that still current?

segments.speaker: patient
segments.text: Still the same. Yes.

segments.speaker: doctor
segments.text: And your phone number, 905-555-0147?

segments.speaker: patient
segments.text: That's the house phone. My wife, Linda, usually answers it.

segments.speaker: doctor
segments.text: That's fine. So, this is your three month diabetes check. How have things been going?

segments.speaker: patient
segments.text: Honestly, not great. The holidays were rough. I've been eating a lot more bread and sweets than I should.

segments.speaker: doctor
segments.text: That's common. Are you still taking the metformin, 1,000 milligrams twice a day?

segments.speaker: patient
segments.text: Mostly. I skip the evening dose sometimes because it upsets my stomach. Maybe three or four times a week I miss it. What kind of stomach upset? Cramping and loose stools, usually an hour or so after I take it.

segments.speaker: doctor
segments.text: Okay. What have your sugars been like at home?

segments.speaker: patient
segments.text: In the mornings they're usually between 8 and 10.

segments.speaker: doctor
segments.text: And exercise?

segments.speaker: patient
segments.text: I walk the dog maybe twice a week, less since it got cold.

segments.speaker: doctor
segments.text: Any chest pain, shortness of breath, or problems with your vision?

segments.speaker: patient
segments.text: No chest pain. My eyes seem fine, but I haven't had an eye exam in about 2 years. The one thing is my feet. Sometimes at night I get tingling in my toes.

segments.speaker: doctor
segments.text: Both feet?

segments.speaker: patient
segments.text: Yes, both.

segments.speaker: doctor
segments.text: Okay. Are you taking any supplements?

segments.speaker: patient
segments.text: My brother-in-law keeps telling me to try cinnamon pills, but I haven't started them.

segments.speaker: doctor
segments.text: I'd hold off on those. There isn't good evidence that they help. Now, your A1C from last week came back at 8.1%. In the spring it was 7.4. So it's going up. It is. Your blood pressure today is 142 over 88, and your weight is 98 kg, up two from last time. On the foot exam, your pulses are good, but sensation with the monofilament is reduced at both big toes. That fits with early nerve changes from diabetes.

segments.speaker: patient
segments.text: That's worrying. It's a sign we should tighten things up. Here's what I'd suggest. First, let's switch your metformin to the extended release form, still 1,000 milligrams twice a day. It's usually easier on the stomach.

segments.speaker: doctor
segments.text: Second, I'd like to add a medication called empagliflozin, 10 milligrams once a day. It lowers sugar and also protects the heart and kidneys. Any side effects? It can cause genital yeast infections and make you pee more. So drink enough water. Third, I'm referring you to the diabetes education program to meet with a dietician and to an eye doctor for a retinal exam. We'll also do kidney function and a urine test today.

segments.speaker: patient
segments.text: And the blood pressure? I'll recheck it at your next visit. If it's still above 130 over 80, we'll start a medication for it. Let's repeat the A1C in three months. Okay. That's a lot, but it makes sense.

segments.speaker: doctor
segments.text: Check your feet every day and call us if you notice any sores. See you in three months, Mr. Mitchell.
